unit.title: Apply knowledge of Team Jamaica requirements in the workplace

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which of these is a topic covered in Team Jamaica training?

Building concrete houses and walls
Running a bank branch and its tellers
Stopping the harassment of visitors

questions.stem: What is the main aim of Team Jamaica training?
options: To teach workers how to build and repair hotels and villas
To help workers give visitors a warm, safe, respectful welcome
To train workers to sell more goods to every visitor they meet
To prepare workers for jobs on cruise ships far from home

questions.stem: In Jamaica, which number do you dial to reach the police in an emergency?

essays.stem: Explain what Team Jamaica is, who it is for, and why it matters to the tourism industry.
essays.modelAnswer: Team Jamaica is a training programme run by TPDCo, the Tourism Product Development Company, for people who work with visitors. It is meant for workers such as hotel and villa staff, tour guides, drivers, craft vendors and attraction staff, as TPDCo's current course sets out. The training covers courtesy and good customer service, the warm Jamaican welcome, visitor safety and security, product knowledge about Jamaica's history, culture and attractions, and how to give harassment-free service. Workers who complete it receive a certificate; how long it lasts and how it is renewed are as TPDCo's current course sets out. It matters because visitors judge Jamaica by the people they meet. When every worker is courteous, honest and well informed, visitors feel safe and welcome, enjoy their stay, tell others and come back. This protects jobs and the good name of Jamaican tourism.
markingPoints: Team Jamaica is run by TPDCo
It is for people who work with visitors (villa and hotel staff, guides, drivers, vendors)
It covers courtesy, visitor safety, knowledge of Jamaica and harassment-free service
Certificate and renewal rules are as TPDCo's current course sets out
Explains why it matters: visitors feel safe and welcome, return and recommend Jamaica

essays.stem: Describe how a villa worker can show courtesy and the warm Jamaican welcome to visitors.
essays.modelAnswer: A villa worker shows courtesy from the first moment. They greet each visitor with a smile and eye contact, say "Good morning" or "Welcome to Jamaica", and use the guest's name and title. They introduce themselves and offer help, such as carrying bags or bringing a cool drink. They listen carefully, speak clearly in simple English, and are patient with questions, even ones they have heard many times. They are honest: they give correct information and say "I will find out" when they are not sure. They respect guests' privacy and never pressure them to buy anything. They share their pride in Jamaica by recommending local food, music, places and licensed tours. Small extra touches, such as remembering a guest's favourite drink or fruit, make the welcome personal. They stay polite even when a guest is difficult, and they thank guests and wish them well when they leave.
markingPoints: Warm greeting with a smile, eye contact and the guest's name
Offers help, listens, speaks clearly and is patient
Gives honest, correct information and finds out when unsure
Respects privacy and never pressures guests
Shares pride in Jamaica, adds personal touches, and says a polite goodbye

essays.stem: Explain what visitor harassment is, give three examples, and explain why it harms Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: Visitor harassment is any behaviour that annoys, pressures, frightens or embarrasses a visitor against their wishes. It often happens when someone will not accept a visitor's "no". Examples are: a vendor following a visitor along the street and blocking their way until they buy something; a person on the beach offering drugs again and again; someone touching a visitor's hair to braid it without being asked; people grabbing visitors' bags at the gate to carry them for money; and rude or sexual remarks shouted at visitors. Harassment harms Jamaica because visitors feel unsafe and uncomfortable. They may stay inside their hotel or villa and spend less money in local communities. They tell family and friends and post bad reviews online, so fewer people choose to visit. This means fewer jobs and less income for Jamaicans, and harm to the country's good name. Some kinds of harassment are also against the law.
markingPoints: Defines harassment: unwanted pressure or behaviour, not accepting "no"
Gives three correct examples
Visitors feel unsafe and spend less in communities
Bad word of mouth and reviews mean fewer visitors
Fewer jobs and less income, harm to Jamaica's name; some harassment is against the law

essays.stem: Describe what a tourism worker should do to prevent harassment, and to help a visitor who is being harassed.
essays.modelAnswer: To prevent harassment, the worker sets a good example: they never pressure guests to buy anything, they offer a service once and accept the answer, and they never touch guests without permission. They give guests advice before they go out: use licensed tours and transport, say a clear and polite "no, thank you" and keep walking, and keep valuables out of sight. They report people who often bother visitors near the villa. If a visitor is being harassed, the worker should stay calm and polite, step in safely, and help the visitor move away, for example by saying "Excuse me, the guest is with me." They should not shout or fight. If the person will not stop, or there is a threat, the worker calls security or the police on 119. Afterwards, they check that the visitor is all right, write down what happened, and tell their supervisor so it can be followed up, as TPDCo's current course sets out.
markingPoints: Sets a good example: no pressure, offers once, no touching
Advises guests before they go out (licensed operators, polite "no, thank you", valuables)
Steps in calmly and safely to help the visitor move away, without shouting or fighting
Calls security or the police (119) if the person will not stop or there is a threat
Checks on the visitor, records what happened and tells the supervisor

essays.stem: Describe the safety advice you would give a family of visitors staying at a beachfront villa.
essays.modelAnswer: I would tell the family to swim only where it is safe, to check the beach flags, and never to swim when a red flag is flying, alone, at night, or after drinking alcohol. Children must be watched at all times near the sea and the villa pool, and the pool gate kept closed. Because the sun is strong, they should use sunscreen, wear hats, drink plenty of water and stay in the shade in the middle of the day. They should keep passports, cash and other valuables in the villa safe, carry only what they need, and lock doors and windows when they go out or go to bed. For trips, they should use licensed tour and transport operators that the villa can recommend, and say a polite "no, thank you" to anyone who pressures them. I would give them the villa's phone number and the emergency numbers: police 119, and fire and ambulance 110.
markingPoints: Swimming safety: flags, never alone, at night or after alcohol
Children watched at all times near the sea and pool; pool gate closed
Sun safety: sunscreen, hats, water, shade at midday
Valuables in the safe; doors and windows locked
Licensed operators, and the emergency numbers (police 119; fire and ambulance 110)

essays.stem: A guest's bag is stolen while they are on an outing. Describe how you would help them.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would make sure the guest is safe and check whether they are hurt. If they are injured, I would get first aid or call an ambulance on 110. I would stay calm, listen, reassure them, and take them to a quiet place. Then I would help them report the theft to the police, by calling 119 or going to the nearest police station, so that they get a police report, which they may need for insurance and for a new passport. I would help them make a list of what was taken. If bank cards were stolen, I would help them contact their bank to block the cards at once. If a passport was taken, I would help them contact their embassy or consulate. I would tell my supervisor and write an incident report. For the rest of their stay, I would check on them, help with calls or transport, and make sure they feel safe again.
markingPoints: Checks the guest is safe and gets first aid or an ambulance (110) if needed
Stays calm and reassures the guest
Helps them report it to the police (119) and get a police report
Helps block bank cards and contact the embassy or consulate for a passport
Tells the supervisor, writes an incident report and follows up

essays.stem: Describe Jamaica's national symbols, and explain how you would share them with a guest.
essays.modelAnswer: Jamaica's flag is black, green and gold, with a gold diagonal cross. The national motto is "Out of Many, One People", which shows that Jamaicans come from many backgrounds but are one nation. The national bird is the doctor bird, a hummingbird with long tail feathers. The national flower is the lignum vitae, with small blue flowers, and the national tree is the blue mahoe. The national fruit is the ackee, and the national dish is ackee and saltfish. Jamaica also has seven National Heroes, including Nanny of the Maroons, Sam Sharpe, Paul Bogle and Marcus Garvey. I would share these with a guest in a friendly way, for example by pointing out a doctor bird in the garden, serving ackee and saltfish at breakfast and explaining it, or telling the story of a National Hero when we pass a monument. I would keep my facts correct and answer questions honestly.
markingPoints: Flag: black, green and gold
Motto "Out of Many, One People" and what it means
National bird, flower and tree named correctly
National fruit and dish, and the seven National Heroes (at least two named)
Shares them in a friendly, correct way, with an example

essays.stem: A guest wants to learn about Jamaican culture. Describe what you could tell them about Jamaican music, food and history.
essays.modelAnswer: For music, I could explain that Jamaica created mento, ska, rocksteady, reggae and dancehall. Reggae was made famous around the world by Bob Marley, and the guest could visit the Bob Marley Museum in Kingston or his birthplace at Nine Mile in St Ann. For food, I could describe jerk chicken and pork, seasoned with scotch bonnet pepper and pimento and cooked slowly over wood; ackee and saltfish, the national dish; curry goat; bammy; festival; patties; and sorrel at Christmas. I would invite them to try local fruit in season. For history, I could tell them that the Taíno were the first people, the Spanish came in 1494, and the British took the island in 1655. Enslaved Africans were forced to work on the sugar estates until slavery ended, with full freedom on 1 August 1838, and the Maroons kept their freedom in the hills. Jamaica became independent on 6 August 1962.
markingPoints: Music: Jamaican styles (ska, reggae, dancehall) and Bob Marley
Food: correct examples of Jamaican dishes and drinks
History: the Taíno, the Spanish (1494) and the British (1655)
Slavery, Emancipation (1 August 1838) and the Maroons
Independence on 6 August 1962, and suggests places to visit

essays.stem: Explain how you would use Team Jamaica principles in your daily work at a villa.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start each day neat and on time, ready to give a warm, professional welcome. I would greet every guest with a smile, use their name, and offer help without being asked. I would answer questions honestly and correctly, and when I am not sure, I would find out from a reliable source. I would share my knowledge of Jamaica, recommending local food, attractions and licensed tours, without pushing guests to buy anything or sending them only to places that pay me. I would give guests safety advice about swimming, the sun, valuables and transport, and know the emergency numbers. I would protect guests from harassment and report anyone who bothers them. I would respect their privacy and property, and treat every guest equally, whatever their background. I would also look after the environment by saving water and power and never littering. In this way, every guest leaves with a good picture of Jamaica.
markingPoints: Neat, on time, and gives a warm, professional welcome
Gives honest, correct information and checks when unsure
Shares knowledge of Jamaica without pressure or hidden payments
Gives safety advice and protects guests from harassment
Respects privacy, treats all guests equally and cares for the environment

essays.stem: Explain why protecting Jamaica's natural environment is part of good tourism service, and what workers and visitors can do.
essays.modelAnswer: Many visitors come to Jamaica for its beaches, coral reefs, rivers, waterfalls, mountains and wildlife. If these are damaged, the island becomes less attractive, fewer visitors come, and jobs are lost. Coral reefs also protect the coast from storms and give homes to fish. So caring for the environment is part of giving visitors a good experience, now and in the future. Workers can set a good example: they never litter, they sort waste and recycle where they can, and they save water and power at the villa, for example by switching off lights and air conditioning in empty rooms. They can explain these practices to guests and recommend licensed nature tours that protect wildlife. Visitors can help by using reef-safe sunscreen, not touching or taking coral or shells, not feeding wild animals, staying on marked trails, and reusing towels. Workers should politely remind guests of these points.
markingPoints: Visitors come for nature; damage means fewer visitors and lost jobs
Reefs protect the coast and support fish
Workers: no litter, sort waste, save water and power
Workers explain green practices and recommend licensed nature tours
Visitors: reef-safe sunscreen, leave coral and shells, do not feed wildlife, stay on trails

practical1.title: Role-play a warm welcome and harassment-free visitor care at a villa
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group four situation cards, for example: welcoming a guest family at the villa gate; a guest being pressured by a vendor outside the gate; a guest asking how to get safely to an attraction; a guest who has lost their passport. For each card, one member plays the villa worker, others play the guests or the vendor, and one member notes what was said. The worker must show Jamaican courtesy, give correct safety advice, and deal with any harassment calmly and safely. After each role play, the worker writes a short note in the villa log: what happened, the advice given, and anything reported. Swap roles so that every member plays the worker at least once. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with the log notes.
materials: Four situation cards from the assessor
A simple villa gate or reception set-up, a phone and a welcome tray
A list of licensed transport and tour operators, or a sample list from the assessor
A villa log book or note sheets
Pens, a clipboard, and a phone or tablet for photos
photos: The group's plan of who plays each part
The welcome role play, showing the greeting
The vendor role play, showing the worker stepping in calmly
checklist: Greeted the guest warmly, with a smile and the guest's name
Spoke clearly and politely, in simple English
Gave correct safety advice (licensed transport, valuables, emergency numbers)
Dealt with the harassment calmly, without shouting or touching, and reported it
Gave honest information and did not pressure the guest
Wrote a clear, accurate log note
Took part respectfully in other members' role plays
safety: Role plays use words only: no pushing, grabbing or touching
Use made-up names, never real people
Any member may stop a role play if they feel uncomfortable
Keep the area clear of trip hazards

practical2.title: Make a 'Know Jamaica' visitor display and a pocket safety card
practical2.brief: Your group makes a display that a villa could put up for its guests, and a small safety card for guests to carry. The display has four parts: Jamaica's national symbols (flag, motto, bird, flower, tree, fruit, dish and the seven National Heroes); a short history timeline, from the Taíno to Independence in 1962; a map showing the 14 parishes and the main resort areas; and local food and music to try. The safety card gives short tips on swimming, the sun, valuables, licensed transport and saying 'no, thank you', plus the emergency numbers (police 119; fire and ambulance 110) and the villa's phone number. Each member makes at least one part, checks its facts against a reliable source, then presents it to the assessor and to 'visitors' (other trainees) and answers one question. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with the display and the safety card.
materials: Poster paper, card, markers, coloured pencils, glue and scissors
Reference books, or a computer, tablet or phone with internet access if the Centre allows
A display board or wall space
photos: The group's plan, showing each member's part
Research and fact-checking with a reliable source
The history timeline and the parish map
checklist: Made at least one part of the display neatly and clearly
Facts are correct (symbols, dates, parishes, emergency numbers)
Checked the facts against a reliable source and recorded it
Presented their part clearly and with pride
Answered a visitor's question correctly and politely
Helped the group finish on time and shared materials fairly
safety: Use scissors carefully and keep them closed when not in use
Keep glue and markers capped, and use them in a ventilated room
Use only websites the Centre allows
Keep walkways clear while building the display
